87: **Fix**: Move detailed content to references/, keep SKILL.md lean.
88: 
89: ### Pitfall 3: Missing Bundled Resources
90: 
91: **Problem**: The agent recreates same code repeatedly instead of using scripts.
92: 
93: **Example**:
94: ```markdown
95: # Bad - No script provided
96: \## HOW IT WORKS
97: Rotate PDF by writing Python code using PyPDF2...
98: 
99: # Good - Script provided
100: \## HOW IT WORKS
101: Use scripts/rotate_pdf.py to rotate PDF files.
102: ```
103: 
104: **Fix**: Identify repeatedly needed code, create scripts.
105: 
106: ### Pitfall 4: Unclear Triggers
107: 
108: **Problem**: Skill exists but never triggers because conditions are unclear.
109: 
110: **Example**:
111: ```markdown
112: # Bad
113: \## 1. WHEN TO USE
114: Use this skill for documents.
115: 
116: # Good
117: \## 1. WHEN TO USE
118: Use this skill when validating markdown files after Write/Edit operations.
119: Manual optimization when:
120: - README needs major AI-friendliness improvements
121: - Creating critical documentation
122: - Quality assurance before sharing
123: ```
124: 
125: **Fix**: Be specific about automatic vs manual triggers, clear use cases.
126: 
127: ### Pitfall 5: Second-Person Language
128: 
129: **Problem**: Skill uses "you" instead of imperative form.
130: 
131: **Example**:
132: ```markdown
133: # Bad
134: You should validate the file before processing.
135: 
136: # Good
137: Validate the file before processing.
138: ```
139: 
140: **Fix**: Use imperative/infinitive form throughout.
141: 
142: ### Pitfall 6: Platform Compatibility
143: 
144: **Problem**: Skill references automatic triggers or platform-specific features that don't work in OpenCode.
145: 
146: **Context**: Skills should be platform-agnostic. OpenCode uses AGENTS.md discipline for enforcement, not automatic triggers.
147: 
148: **Example**:
149: ```markdown
150: # Bad - Claims automatic behavior
151: #### Automatic Enforcement
152: Enforcement runs automatically via triggers:
153: - After Write/Edit operations
154: - Before AI processes prompts
155: 
156: # Good - Manual workflow documentation
157: #### Validation Workflow
158: **Filename Validation** (after Write/Edit operations):
159: - Purpose: Filename enforcement
160: - Apply: After creating or editing files
161: - Verify: Before claiming completion
162: ```
163: 
164: **Fix**: When documenting enforcement features:
165: 1. Replace "runs automatically" with "verify manually"
166: 2. Replace "blocks commits" with "verify before commits"
167: 3. Replace "Automatic activation" with "Use this skill when"
168: 4. Focus on AGENTS.md discipline, not automatic triggers
169: 
170: **Validation Check**: Search for outdated patterns before packaging:
171: ```bash
172: grep -E "runs automatically|blocks commits|Automatic.*via|auto-enforced" SKILL.md
173: ```
174: 
175: ### Pitfall 7: Multiline YAML Description
176: 
177: **Problem**: Skill description uses YAML multiline block format which isn't parsed correctly.
178: 
179: **Example**:
180: ```yaml
181: # Bad - Multiline block format (parser fails)
182: description:
183:   This is my skill description
184:   spanning multiple lines.
185: 
186: # Good - Single line after colon
187: description: This is my skill description all on one line.
188: ```
189: 
190: **Cause**: Prettier and other formatters may auto-format long descriptions to multiline.
191: 
192: **Fix**: Keep description on a single line after the colon. If a formatter changes it, manually revert.
193: 
194: ### Pitfall 8: File References in Wrong Section or Redundant Navigation Guide
195: 
196: **Problem**: File references placed in "WHEN TO USE" section, or routing logic duplicated across multiple tables/snippets.
197: 
198: **Example**:
199: ```markdown
200: # Bad - File references in "When to Use"
201: \## 1. WHEN TO USE
202: See `references/guide.md` for details...
203: 
204: # Bad - Separate lookup table duplicates router logic
205: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
206: 
207: ### Routing Table
208: | Intent     | Path                           |
209: | ---------- | ------------------------------ |
210: | Validation | `references/core-standards.md` |
211: 
212: ### Smart Router Pseudocode
213: ...
214: 
215: # Good - Short prose in Section 2, pseudocode in the sibling router file
216: \## 1. WHEN TO USE
217: 
218: ### Activation Triggers
219: - User requests validation...
220: 
221: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
222: 
223: Use this skill when a request needs a document validated.
224: Check the detection signal first, then load one resource domain.
225: The router block that loads resources sits in `ROUTER.md`.
226: 
227: \## 3. HOW IT WORKS
228: ...
229: 
230: # ROUTER.md
231: 
232: \## MACHINE ROUTER
233: 
234: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"validate": ["validate", "check"]}
235: RESOURCE_MAP = {"validate": "references/core-standards.md"}
236: 
237: def discover_markdown_resources(): ...
238: 
239: **Rule**:
240: ```
241: "When to Use" = WHEN (triggers, conditions, use cases)
242: "Smart Routing" = HOW a prompt reaches the skill, in 8 to 12 lines of prose
243: "MACHINE ROUTER" = the pseudocode that loads resources, in the last H2 section of `ROUTER.md`
244: 
245: ⚠️ ANTI-PATTERN: Do NOT duplicate routing logic in separate lookup tables
246: ⚠️ ANTI-PATTERN: Do NOT put the router block inside SMART ROUTING
247: ```
248: 
249: **Fix**: Keep Section 2 to 8 to 12 lines of prose, put one machine router block in the sibling `ROUTER.md` under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading, and link to that file from `SKILL.md`.
250: 
251: ### Pitfall 9: Router Section Left in SKILL.md, or a Missing Router File
252: 
253: **Problem**: The machine router sits inside SMART ROUTING, or a skill keeps its `MACHINE ROUTER` section in `SKILL.md` instead of a sibling `ROUTER.md`.
254: 
255: **Example**:
256: ```markdown
257: # Bad - Router block inside Section 2
258: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
259: [prose, then the whole router block]
260: 
261: # Bad - Router section still inline
262: parent-hub/example-packet/
263:   SKILL.md
264:   \## MACHINE ROUTER
265:   [the router block]
266: 
267: # Good - Packet keeps its router in the sibling file
268: parent-hub/example-packet/
269:   SKILL.md            # short SMART ROUTING prose with a link to ./ROUTER.md
270:   ROUTER.md           # the router block under a final ## MACHINE ROUTER heading
271: ```
272: 
273: **Fix**: Move the block into the sibling `ROUTER.md` under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading, and add the relative link to `./ROUTER.md` in `SKILL.md`. Every skill and every mode packet owns that file. `package_skill.py --strict` reports a leftover section as RS-002, a missing or escaping file as RS-004, and a missing link as RS-005.

24:

36: 
37: ## 2. SKILL ANATOMY
38: 
39: Every skill has a required `SKILL.md` root marker plus class-specific root metadata; the human-facing README and bundled content resources are optional:
40: 
41: ```
42: skill-name/
43: ├── SKILL.md (required)
44: │   ├── YAML frontmatter metadata (required)
45: │   │   ├── name: (required)
46: │   │   └── description: (required)
47: │   └── Markdown instructions (required)
48: ├── README.md (optional, human-facing orientation)
49: └── Bundled Resources (optional)
50:     ├── scripts/          - Executable code (Python/Bash/etc.)
51:     ├── references/       - Documentation (flat or domain subfolders)
52:     └── assets/           - Files used in output (subfolders OK for organization)
53:         ├── skill/         - Skill creation templates (SKILL.md, README, reference, asset)
54:         ├── agents/        - Agent and command creation templates
55:         └── readme/ - README-shaped scaffolds (README, install guide)
56: ```
57: 
58: The content directories shown here are optional, but root metadata is not; use the [skill-root-metadata-contract.md](./skill-root-metadata-contract.md) matrix for the class-specific authored and generated files.
59: 
60: **Folder Organization Principle**:
61: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills
62:   - Grouped example: `references/core-standards.md`, `references/validation.md`
63:   - Domain example: `references/backend/go/`, `references/frontend/react/`
64: - **assets/** = Subfolders ALLOWED when organizing many files by category
65:   - Group related templates together for clarity
66:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
67: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections
68: 
69: ### SKILL.md Requirements
70: 
71: **Metadata Quality**: The `name` and `description` in YAML frontmatter determine when the AI agent will use the skill. Be specific about what the skill does and when to use it.
72: 
73: **Writing Style Guidelines**:
74: - Use **third-person** in descriptions (e.g., "This skill should be used when..." instead of "Use this skill when...")
75: - Write using **imperative/infinitive form** (verb-first instructions), not second person
76: - Use objective, instructional language (e.g., "To accomplish X, do Y" rather than "You should do X")
77: - Keep SKILL.md body under **5k words**
78: 
79: **Required Sections** (enforced by markdown-document-specialist validation):
80: 1. WHEN TO USE (activation triggers and use cases ONLY)
81: 2. SMART ROUTING (8 to 12 lines of plain prose: what selects this skill, what it loads first, where the machine router is)
82: 3. HOW IT WORKS
83: 4. RULES (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
84: 5. REFERENCES (or combined `SMART ROUTING & REFERENCES`)
85: 
86: Validation reminder:
87: - `scripts/package_skill.py` fails if `REFERENCES` is missing and no approved combined heading variant is present.
88: 
89: ### README.md Guidance
90: 
91: Create `README.md` when the skill needs human-facing orientation beyond runtime routing. Use [skill-readme-template.md](../../assets/skill/skill-readme-template.md) for skill package READMEs rather than the generic folder README template.
92: 
93: Include a skill README when:
94: - Operators need a quick start, examples, troubleshooting or FAQ.
95: - The skill has multiple modes, resource domains, scripts or validation commands.
96: - Readers need a concise map that explains how `SKILL.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` fit together.
97: 
98: Keep boundaries clear:
99: - `SKILL.md` is the runtime instruction and routing surface.
100: - `README.md` is the human orientation and navigation surface.
101: - Long conceptual depth belongs in focused `references/` files.
102: 
103: **Recommended Sections**:
104: 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
105: 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
106: 8. RELATED RESOURCES
107: 
108: ### Routing Authority Standard
109: 
110: The machine router is the authoritative routing source. It sits in the sibling `ROUTER.md`, in a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` section that is the last H2 of that file. Section 2 of `SKILL.md` stays short prose that links to it. Do not maintain separate use-case routing tables.
111: 
112: Router parity checklist for the machine router block:
113: - Guarded in-skill loading (`_guard_in_skill`)
114: - Recursive markdown discovery (`discover_markdown_resources`)
115: - Weighted intent scoring (`score_intents`)
116: - Ambiguity handling (`select_intents`)
117: - Explicit loading levels with ON_DEMAND triggers
118: - Optional `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST` for low-confidence requests
119: 
120: Smart-router resilience reference:
121: - Use [skill-smart-router.md](../../assets/skill/skill-smart-router.md) as the canonical pattern for runtime markdown discovery, guarded existence-checked loading, extensible routing keys, and multi-tier fallback behavior.
122: - Preserve each skill's domain-specific intent model, resource map, and loading levels; only standardize discovery, loading, routing-key, and fallback mechanics.
123: 
124: **Section Boundary Rules:**
125: ```
126: ❌ WRONG: File references or routing logic in "WHEN TO USE"
127: ❌ WRONG: Separate use-case routing tables or navigation guides
128: ❌ WRONG: A machine router block inside SMART ROUTING
129: ✅ RIGHT: Short routing prose in Section 2, one machine router block in the final MACHINE ROUTER section of ROUTER.md
130: 
131: "WHEN TO USE" = WHEN (triggers, conditions, use cases)
132: "SMART ROUTING" = HOW a prompt reaches this skill, in 8 to 12 lines of prose
133: "MACHINE ROUTER" = the pseudocode that loads resources (authoritative)
134: ```
135: 
136: ### Bundled Resources (Optional)
137: 
138: #### Scripts Directory (`scripts/`)
139: 
140: Executable code for tasks requiring deterministic reliability or repeatedly rewritten.
141: 
142: **When to include scripts**:
143: - Same code being rewritten repeatedly by the agent
144: - Deterministic reliability needed
145: - Performance optimization required
146: - Complex logic better handled by programming language
147: 
148: **Examples**:
149: - `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` - PDF rotation tasks
150: - `scripts/extract_structure.py` - Document structure extraction
151: - `scripts/init_skill.py` - Skill scaffolding
152: 
153: **Benefits**:
154: - Token efficient (may execute without loading into context)
155: - Deterministic behavior
156: - Reusable across skill invocations
157: 
158: **Note**: Scripts may still need to be read for patching or environment adjustments.
159: 
160: #### References Directory (`references/`)
161: 
162: Documentation loaded as needed to inform the agent's process and thinking.
163: 
164: **When to include references**:
165: - Documentation the agent should reference while working
166: - Detailed domain knowledge
167: - API specifications
168: - Database schemas
169: - Company policies
170: 
171: **Examples**:
172: - `references/schema.md` - Database schema documentation
173: - `references/api-docs.md` - API endpoint specifications
174: - `references/policies.md` - Company policies and guidelines
175: - `sk-create-quality-control/references/workflows.md` - Detailed workflow documentation
176: 
177: **Benefits**:
178: - Keeps SKILL.md lean
179: - Loaded only when needed
180: - Supports deep, detailed documentation
181: 
182: **Best practice**:
183: - If files are large (>10k words), include grep search patterns in SKILL.md
184: - Avoid duplication between SKILL.md and references
185: - Keep only essential instructions in SKILL.md
186: - Move detailed reference material to references files
187: 
188: **Frontmatter contract**: every reference and asset markdown file carries the full 5-field block (`title`, `description`, `trigger_phrases` 3-8, `importance_tier`, `contextType`); `README.md` files are exempt. The Skill Advisor harvests these fields as routing signal — see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for the template and field rules.
189: 
190: #### Assets Directory (`assets/`)
191: 
192: Files used within the output the agent produces (not loaded into context).
193: 
194: **When to include assets**:
195: - Skill needs files for final output
196: - Templates for document generation
197: - Boilerplate code
198: - Images, icons, logos
199: 
200: **Examples**:
201: - `assets/logo.png` - Brand logo
202: - `assets/template.html` - HTML template
203: - `assets/font.ttf` - Custom font
204: - `assets/frontmatter-templates.md` - YAML frontmatter examples
205: 
206: **Benefits**:
207: - Separates output resources from documentation
208: - Keeps context window clean
209: - Provides consistent output resources
210: 
211: ---
212: 
213: ## 3. SKILL STRUCTURE SYSTEM
214: 
215: ### Why Layered Skill Docs
216: 
217: Large skills eventually outgrow one `SKILL.md` file. The maintainable pattern is to keep routing in `SKILL.md` and split depth into focused reference files that can be loaded on demand.
218: 
219: ### Core Structure
220: 
221: ```
222: skill-name/
223: ├── SKILL.md                # Primary entrypoint (activation rules, routing, core behavior)
224: ├── references/
225: │   ├── topic-a.md
226: │   ├── topic-b.md
227: │   └── topic-c.md
228: ├── assets/
229: └── scripts/
230: ```
231: 
232: ### Design Logic
233: 
234: 1. Start with `SKILL.md` for trigger/routing behavior.
235: 2. Use `README.md` or the SKILL navigation section as a concise map.
236: 3. Load only the specific `references/` files required by the active task.
237: 4. Keep progressive disclosure strict to control context size.
238: 
239: ### How AI Should Use Layered Skills
240: 
241: Use this operating pattern:
242: 
243: 1. Read `SKILL.md` for trigger and routing rules.
244: 2. Open `README.md` if additional navigation is needed.
245: 3. Read one focused reference at a time and summarize locally.
246: 4. Follow markdown links only when they advance the current objective.
247: 5. Stop once confidence is high and required context is complete.
248: 
249: ### Authoring Rules
250: 
251: - Keep each reference file scoped to one complete concept.
252: - Keep reference content concise and practical.
253: - Add one-line YAML `description` to long-form docs.
254: - Put links inside meaningful prose, not isolated link dumps.
255: - Validate markdown links after edits.
256: 
257: ### Templates
258: 
259: Use these templates when authoring layered skills:
260: - Skill template: `../../assets/skill/skill-md-template.md`
261: - Skill README template: `../../assets/skill/skill-readme-template.md`
262: - Reference template: `../../assets/skill/skill-reference-template.md`
263: - Asset template: `../../assets/skill/skill-asset-template.md`
264:

94: - Operators need a quick start, examples, troubleshooting or FAQ.
95: - The skill has multiple modes, resource domains, scripts or validation commands.
96: - Readers need a concise map that explains how `SKILL.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` fit together.
97: 
98: Keep boundaries clear:
99: - `SKILL.md` is the runtime instruction and routing surface.
100: - `README.md` is the human orientation and navigation surface.
101: - Long conceptual depth belongs in focused `references/` files.
102: 
103: **Recommended Sections**:
104: 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
105: 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
106: 8. RELATED RESOURCES
107: 
108: ### Routing Authority Standard
109: 
110: The machine router is the authoritative routing source. It sits in the sibling `ROUTER.md`, in a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` section that is the last H2 of that file. Section 2 of `SKILL.md` stays short prose that links to it. Do not maintain separate use-case routing tables.
111: 
112: Router parity checklist for the machine router block:
113: - Guarded in-skill loading (`_guard_in_skill`)
114: - Recursive markdown discovery (`discover_markdown_resources`)
115: - Weighted intent scoring (`score_intents`)
116: - Ambiguity handling (`select_intents`)
117: - Explicit loading levels with ON_DEMAND triggers
118: - Optional `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST` for low-confidence requests
119: 
120: Smart-router resilience reference:
121: - Use [skill-smart-router.md](../../assets/skill/skill-smart-router.md) as the canonical pattern for runtime markdown discovery, guarded existence-checked loading, extensible routing keys, and multi-tier fallback behavior.
122: - Preserve each skill's domain-specific intent model, resource map, and loading levels; only standardize discovery, loading, routing-key, and fallback mechanics.
123: 
124: **Section Boundary Rules:**
125: ```
126: ❌ WRONG: File references or routing logic in "WHEN TO USE"
127: ❌ WRONG: Separate use-case routing tables or navigation guides
128: ❌ WRONG: A machine router block inside SMART ROUTING
129: ✅ RIGHT: Short routing prose in Section 2, one machine router block in the final MACHINE ROUTER section of ROUTER.md
130: 
131: "WHEN TO USE" = WHEN (triggers, conditions, use cases)
132: "SMART ROUTING" = HOW a prompt reaches this skill, in 8 to 12 lines of prose
133: "MACHINE ROUTER" = the pseudocode that loads resources (authoritative)
134: ```
135: 
136: ### Bundled Resources (Optional)
137: 
138: #### Scripts Directory (`scripts/`)
139: 
140: Executable code for tasks requiring deterministic reliability or repeatedly rewritten.
141: 
142: **When to include scripts**:
143: - Same code being rewritten repeatedly by the agent
144: - Deterministic reliability needed
145: - Performance optimization required
146: - Complex logic better handled by programming language
147: 
148: **Examples**:
149: - `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` - PDF rotation tasks
150: - `scripts/extract_structure.py` - Document structure extraction
151: - `scripts/init_skill.py` - Skill scaffolding
152: 
153: **Benefits**:
154: - Token efficient (may execute without loading into context)
155: - Deterministic behavior
156: - Reusable across skill invocations
157: 
158: **Note**: Scripts may still need to be read for patching or environment adjustments.
159: 
160: #### References Directory (`references/`)
161: 
162: Documentation loaded as needed to inform the agent's process and thinking.
163: 
164: **When to include references**:
165: - Documentation the agent should reference while working
166: - Detailed domain knowledge
167: - API specifications
168: - Database schemas
169: - Company policies
170: 
171: **Examples**:
172: - `references/schema.md` - Database schema documentation
173: - `references/api-docs.md` - API endpoint specifications
174: - `references/policies.md` - Company policies and guidelines
175: - `sk-create-quality-control/references/workflows.md` - Detailed workflow documentation
176: 
177: **Benefits**:
178: - Keeps SKILL.md lean
179: - Loaded only when needed
180: - Supports deep, detailed documentation
181: 
182: **Best practice**:
183: - If files are large (>10k words), include grep search patterns in SKILL.md
184: - Avoid duplication between SKILL.md and references
185: - Keep only essential instructions in SKILL.md
186: - Move detailed reference material to references files
187:

The Skill Advisor harvests these fields as routing signal — see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for the template and field rules.
189: 
190: #### Assets Directory (`assets/`)
191: 
192: Files used within the output the agent produces (not loaded into context).
193: 
194: **When to include assets**:
195: - Skill needs files for final output
196: - Templates for document generation
197: - Boilerplate code
198: - Images, icons, logos
199: 
200: **Examples**:
201: - `assets/logo.png` - Brand logo
202: - `assets/template.html` - HTML template
203: - `assets/font.ttf` - Custom font
204: - `assets/frontmatter-templates.md` - YAML frontmatter examples
205: 
206: **Benefits**:
207: - Separates output resources from documentation
208: - Keeps context window clean
209: - Provides consistent output resources
210:

213: ## 3. SKILL STRUCTURE SYSTEM
214: 
215: ### Why Layered Skill Docs
216: 
217: Large skills eventually outgrow one `SKILL.md` file. The maintainable pattern is to keep routing in `SKILL.md` and split depth into focused reference files that can be loaded on demand.
218: 
219: ### Core Structure
220: 
221: ```
222: skill-name/
223: ├── SKILL.md                # Primary entrypoint (activation rules, routing, core behavior)
224: ├── references/
225: │   ├── topic-a.md
226: │   ├── topic-b.md
227: │   └── topic-c.md
228: ├── assets/
229: └── scripts/
230: ```
231: 
232: ### Design Logic
233: 
234: 1. Start with `SKILL.md` for trigger/routing behavior.
235: 2. Use `README.md` or the SKILL navigation section as a concise map.
236: 3. Load only the specific `references/` files required by the active task.
237: 4. Keep progressive disclosure strict to control context size.
238: 
239: ### How AI Should Use Layered Skills
240: 
241: Use this operating pattern:
242: 
243: 1. Read `SKILL.md` for trigger and routing rules.
244: 2. Open `README.md` if additional navigation is needed.
245: 3. Read one focused reference at a time and summarize locally.
246: 4. Follow markdown links only when they advance the current objective.
247: 5. Stop once confidence is high and required context is complete.
248: 
249: ### Authoring Rules
250: 
251: - Keep each reference file scoped to one complete concept.
252: - Keep reference content concise and practical.
253: - Add one-line YAML `description` to long-form docs.
254: - Put links inside meaningful prose, not isolated link dumps.
255: - Validate markdown links after edits.
256: 
257: ### Templates
258:

261: - Skill README template: `../../assets/skill/skill-readme-template.md`
262: - Reference template: `../../assets/skill/skill-reference-template.md`

Every hub and every mode packet owns the `ROUTER.md` in its own folder. The hub root's file is the stage-two control document, and a packet's file holds that packet's machine router under its `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading. A packet's `SKILL.md` keeps only short routing prose and a link to it, so a router edit belongs in the `ROUTER.md`, never in `SKILL.md`.

A `metadata` mode's vocabulary reaches the advisor **only** through the hub's `graph-metadata.json`. A `lexical` or `alias-fold` mode also needs its projection maps and scorer entries. A stage-one hit with no stage-two intent, or the reverse, means the two disagree about the same phrasing: fix both sides, not the one that happens to be failing.

**The failure this prevents:** concluding the advisor is broken because it does not surface a nested mode by name. It is not broken. It was never going to.

---

## 2. REGISTERED IS NOT ROUTED

Before saying a mode is integrated, confirm every surface carries it. The authoritative list, with what each one breaks, is section 7 of `parent-skills-nested-packets.md`, which `sk-doc` routes to.

The two most often missed:

- The hub's own `SKILL.md` mode table. It is the discovery surface a runtime shows when the advisor is unreachable.
- The runtime command mirrors. A command present in one runtime tree and absent from three is unreachable from those three.

**A green gate is not integration.** The per-hub gate covers some surfaces and asserts only presence, never reachability. Several surfaces have no gate at all.

**The failure this prevents:** reporting "the registries are correct" after checking that entries exist rather than that the policy is complete, or reading a green gate as proof a request can reach the mode.

---

## 5. WHERE THE DETAIL LIVES

This rule carries the discipline. The mechanics belong to the skills that own them.

| Question | Read |
|----------|------|
| What must a new mode land on, and in what order | `parent-skills-nested-packets.md` §7 |
| Hub doctrine, one identity, the `routingClass` table, where each `ROUTER.md` lives | `parent-skills-nested-packets.md` §1-2 |
| Which metadata file is required or forbidden at which root | `skill-root-metadata-contract.md` |
| How the advisor scores, and its regression corpus | the skill-advisor system skill |
| Authoring or repairing a hub | `sk-doc` → `sk-create-skill` |

## 6. SELF-CHECK

A **job** is a process the assistant follows (a workflow mode) or a read-only evidence base it loads beside that process (a surface packet). Two quality-gate checklists in the same `SKILL.md` are still one job. Implement versus review, or two different surface evidence sets, are distinct jobs.

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and needs orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.
161: 
162: ````markdown
163: ---
164: title: "[PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]"
165: description: "[One-sentence description]"
166: trigger_phrases:
167:   - "[search phrase]"
168: version: 1.0.0.0
169: ---
170: 
171: # [PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]
172: 
173: > [One-sentence purpose statement.]
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 1. OVERVIEW
178: 
179: [Explain what this is, who it is for and why it exists.]
180: 
181: ### Key Statistics
182: 
183: | Metric | Value |
184: |---|---|
185: | Status | [Current state] |
186: | Version | [Version or release channel] |
187: | Main audience | [Who uses this] |
188: | Operating modes | [Mode count or short list] |
189: 
190: ### How This Compares
191: 
192: | Capability | This Project | Related Option |
193: |---|---|---|
194: | [Capability] | [Current behavior] | [Difference] |
195: 
196: 
197: ---
198: 
199: ## 2. QUICK START
200: 
201: ```bash
202: # Install or prepare
203: [command]
204: 
205: # Verify
206: [command]
207: ```
208: 
209: Expected result: [what success looks like].
210: 
211: 
212: ---
213: 
214: ## 3. FEATURES
215: 
216: ### Key Features
217: 
218: | Feature | What It Does |
219: |---|---|
220: | [Feature] | [Current behavior] |
221: 
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ## 4. REQUIREMENTS
226: 
227: | Requirement | Minimum | Notes |
228: |---|---|---|
229: | [Runtime or tool] | [Version] | [Why it is needed] |
230: 
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 5. STRUCTURE
235: 
236: ```text
237: [root]/
238: +-- [path]/        # [Purpose]
239: `-- [file]         # [Purpose]
240: ```
241: 
242: | Path | Purpose |
243: |---|---|
244: | `[path]` | [Role] |
245: 
246: <!-- For items needing more than one line, use the itemized pattern
247:      from Section 4 instead of this table. -->
248: 
249: 
250: ---
251: 
252: ## 6. CONFIGURATION
253: 
254: | Option | Default | Purpose |
255: |---|---|---|
256: | `[OPTION]` | `[value]` | [What it controls] |
257: 
258: 
259: ---
260: 
261: ## 7. USAGE EXAMPLES
262: 
263: ```bash
264: [command]
265: ```
266: 
267: Result: [expected output or behavior].
268: 
269: 
270: ---
271: 
272: ## 8. TROUBLESHOOTING
273: 
274: | What You See | Cause | Fix |
275: |---|---|---|
276: | [Symptom] | [Cause] | [Action] |
277: 
278: 
279: ---
280: 
281: ## 9. FAQ
282: 
283: **Q: [Question readers ask often]?**
284: 
285: A: [Short answer with a link when useful.]
286: 
287: 
288: ---
289: 
290: ## 10. RELATED RESOURCES
291: 
292: ### Related Skills
293: 
294: | Skill | Relationship | Use When |
295: |---|---|---|
296: | [`[skill-name]`](../skill-name/SKILL.md) | [Sibling or dependency] | [When to use it] |
297: 
298: ### Related Documents
299: 
300: | Document | Purpose |
301: |---|---|
302: | [`[Document]`](./path/to/doc.md) | [Why it matters] |
303: 
304: ````
305: 
306: ---
307: 
308: ## 7. VALIDATION CHECKLIST
309: 
310: - [ ] README type is correct. Code folders use `readme-code-template.md`.
311: - [ ] Included sections match the audience and task.
312: - [ ] No empty sections remain.
313: - [ ] Commands were tested or marked as examples.
314: - [ ] Links use correct relative paths.
315: - [ ] Frontmatter is valid if present.
316: - [ ] No Table of Contents and no `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments.
317: - [ ] HVR passes: no em dashes, semicolons, banned words or setup phrases.
318: 
319: ---
320: 
321: ## 8. RELATED RESOURCES
322: 
323: - [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) - Code-folder README scaffold.
324: - [`SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md) - README workflow and reference map.
325: - [`core-standards.md`](../../shared/references/core-standards.md) - Markdown formatting rules.
326: - [`validation.md`](../../shared/references/validation.md) - Document validation and DQI scoring.
327: - [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md) - Human Voice Rules.

# Advisor Index Handoff

The shared field vocabulary that `/create:skill`, `/create:skill-parent`, `/doctor:skill-advisor tune`, and `/doctor:skill-advisor parent-skill` all render after touching a skill root, so that scaffolding a skill and diagnosing its advisor state describe the same reality in the same words.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

**Core Principle**: One vocabulary, not one formatter. Create and doctor are separate prompt-asset workflows with genuinely different result shapes (create reports a scaffold; doctor reports a mutating, phase-gated diagnostic run) — see `research.md` Theme F1/F2 in `035-create-doctor-skill-advisor-alignment/001-research/`. What must stay identical across both is the field names, the metadata-ownership statements, and the verification-state enum below, not the surrounding prose or layout.

**When to Use**:
- Wiring a create or doctor workflow asset's completion/report section (A5 in `002-core-alignment-fixes/plan.md`)
- Writing a contract test that pins the shared vocabulary across adapters (A6)
- Deciding whether a given create branch renders the full handoff or the narrow leaf-freshness signal only (§4)

> **Advisor refresh is always operator-owned.** No `/create:*` or `/doctor:*` workflow calls `skill_graph_scan` or `advisor_rebuild` as a side effect of scaffolding or diagnosing a skill. Every workflow that touches a skill root reports refresh status as `NOT RUN` and prints the exact command the operator would run — never chains it automatically (research.md Theme B1/B7, "Questions Answered").

# Upgrading a Customized Skill to v4

Adopters who customized `sk-code` (their stack) or `sk-git` (their conventions) use this guide to decide whether that skill becomes a parent hub or stays a single skill. Most other skills in this framework are internals and need no adopter work.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

v4 reshaped `sk-code` into a parent hub: one advisor identity that dispatches to nested workflow-mode packets and read-only surface packets. `sk-git` stayed a single skill. This file is the adopter-facing path for reconciling a customized copy with that split.

**Core Principle**: Convert a skill into a parent hub only when it has two or more distinct jobs. Keep it single when it has one job. You may also drop the repo's parent `sk-code` and keep your own single skill.

**When to Use**:
- You customized `sk-code` or `sk-git` and a framework update now ships a different shape
- You are deciding whether a flat skill should become a parent hub
- You want to keep a customized skill single and avoid a false migration

What must stay identical across both is the field names, the metadata-ownership statements, and the verification-state enum below, not the surrounding prose or layout.

**When to Use**:
- Wiring a create or doctor workflow asset's completion/report section (A5 in `002-core-alignment-fixes/plan.md`)
- Writing a contract test that pins the shared vocabulary across adapters (A6)

> **Advisor refresh is always operator-owned.** No `/create:*` or `/doctor:*` workflow calls `skill_graph_scan` or `advisor_rebuild` as a side effect of scaffolding or diagnosing a skill. Every workflow that touches a skill root reports refresh status as `NOT RUN` and prints the exact command the operator would run — never chains it automatically (research.md Theme B1/B7, "Questions Answered").

# Upgrading a Customized Skill to v4

Adopters who customized `sk-code` (their stack) or `sk-git` (their conventions) use this guide to decide whether that skill becomes a parent hub or stays a single skill. Most other skills in this framework are internals and need no adopter work.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

v4 reshaped `sk-code` into a parent hub: one advisor identity that dispatches to nested workflow-mode packets and read-only surface packets. `sk-git` stayed a single skill. This file is the adopter-facing path for reconciling a customized copy with that split.

**Core Principle**: Convert a skill into a parent hub only when it has two or more distinct jobs. Keep it single when it has one job. You may also drop the repo's parent `sk-code` and keep your own single skill.

**When to Use**:
- You customized `sk-code` or `sk-git` and a framework update now ships a different shape
- You are deciding whether a flat skill should become a parent hub
- You want to keep a customized skill single and avoid a false migration

The gate runs for a hub root, a standalone skill root and every mode packet a hub declares, and its messages name the skill it checked.

  A standalone skill or a packet declares `router_state: active`, because `stage1-only` is a hub state with no mode registry to stage against, and it is held to the maps it declares rather than to the hub's pair.

  Three deliberate patterns are open to it and closed to a hub:

  - It may route by pseudocode alone with no map at all, which suits a skill that loads its whole reference set on any match.
  - Its `RESOURCE_MAP` may omit a key, or map it to an empty list, only when `NO_LOAD_INTENTS` names that key.
